name: Fashion Collection Launch Lookbook
description: An editorial collection-launch system that carries one seasonal point of view from inspiration and material direction through hero looks, wearing occasions, market phases, and commercial targets.
style_guide:
# Fashion Collection Launch Lookbook

## Design intent

Create an editorial yet commercially useful seasonal collection deck for fashion houses, independent labels, apparel teams, buyers, press, and launch partners. The visual language is warm and tactile: raw-linen paper, camel and terracotta accents, charred-ink typography, restrained italic gestures, full-length studio fashion imagery, fabric macro photography, silhouette diagrams, and carefully paced commercial evidence.

The deck should preserve a clear design point of view while explaining how the collection becomes product, assortment, wearing occasion, market story, and revenue. The reference previews are visual-language examples only. Do not copy their fashion house, season, creative concept, palette names, fabrics, garment designs, models, prices, personas, cities, release dates, wholesale plan, or targets.

## Canvas and grid

- Use a fixed `1280 × 720 px` 16:9 canvas with `58–68 px` side margins, a `28–36 px` collection header, and a `22–28 px` footer for image credits or commercial notes.
- Use a 12-column grid with `18–24 px` gutters. Align image crops, palette swatches, fabric rows, silhouette diagrams, look numbers, occasion cards, launch phases, and commercial metrics.
- Reserve `95–130 px` for chapter label, editorial headline, and short framing text. Let photographs or a single design board occupy the remaining visual field.
- Prefer `6/6` editorial cover splits, `5/7` story-and-moodboard layouts, three-part design-direction pages, three-look rows, and full-width launch plans.
- Use `22–30 px` between major modules and `10–16 px` within product or commercial cards.
- Negative space should feel deliberate and gallery-like. Do not fill open areas with ornamental marks or repeated logos.

## Color system

### Core palette

- Raw linen: `#F1E8D6`. Use for the primary canvas and quiet garment-description fields.
- Soft cream: `#FBF7EF`. Use for inset cards, captions, and image borders.
- Camel: `#AD8257`. Use for secondary surfaces, commercial bands, material context, and a neutral seasonal accent.
- Terracotta: `#C96637`. Use for chapter numbers, launch milestones, selected look details, and the season's active warmth.
- Burnt sienna: `#8D371E`. Use for high-priority editorial emphasis, signature pieces, and selected commercial values.
- Charred ink: `#1F1B19`. Use for primary typography, dark silhouette panels, persona panels, and decisive totals.
- Warm stone: `#8A8175`. Use for captions, secondary labels, rules, and photo credits.

### Semantic use

- Terracotta and burnt sienna communicate the season's design direction, not positive or negative performance by themselves.
- Charred panels should mark an anchor piece, persona, or major commercial readout and remain scarce.
- If financial status needs green or red, use muted tones and label the meaning; do not disrupt the collection palette.
- Preserve accurate garment and material color. Do not force every photograph into the exact slide palette when doing so misrepresents the product.

## Typography

- Use `Helvetica Neue`, `Aptos`, `Inter`, or another clean editorial sans-serif.
- Use a restrained italic cut for one phrase in major headlines, the collection theme, material descriptors, or an anchor-piece note. Avoid script and faux-fashion display fonts.
- Cover title: `52–66 px`, regular. Chapter headline: `32–42 px`, regular. Chapter number: `28–38 px`, italic, terracotta. Labels: `9–11 px`, uppercase, tracked. Body: `14–17 px`. Look captions and tables: `10–13 px`. Credits: `8–10 px`.
- Keep collection numbers, look numbers, prices, style codes, and dates in tabular or consistently aligned numerals.
- Use short editorial statements rather than dense paragraphs. Product information should remain precise and scannable.

## Components

- Cards are flat cream, camel, terracotta, or charred rectangles with thin warm rules, little or no corner radius, and no shadows.
- Palette modules include named swatch, accurate color value or production reference when available, role, and proportional use.
- Fabric rows include composition, weight, mill or supplier status, finish, certification when relevant, cost or MOQ only when approved, and intended garment family.
- Look cards pair one consistent image crop with look number, garment names, material, color, price or range when approved, and launch role.
- Occasion cards explain wardrobe job, share of assortment or buy only when evidenced, and linked hero pieces.
- Commercial KPI cards state target or actual, currency, period, channel, and scenario.

## Charts and diagrams

- Favor moodboards, palette systems, fabric-program tables, simplified silhouette diagrams, hero-look grids, assortment or occasion matrices, phased launch timelines, channel-mix bands, sell-through targets, and door or placement summaries.
- Moodboards should show a coherent light, texture, gesture, material, and cultural reference rather than an unedited collage.
- Silhouette diagrams need consistent body reference, scale, line weight, and garment-length logic. They are design communication, not technical specification.
- Assortment views must define whether percentages refer to styles, units, buy value, floor space, or revenue.
- Launch timelines should include design freeze, sampling, costing, order, production, wholesale, press, campaign, delivery, launch, and review gates as relevant.
- Avoid 3D charts, glossy funnels, decorative trend arrows, and data visualizations that compete with the garments.

## Composition families

### Editorial lookbook cover

Use a raw-linen title field beside one full-height studio portrait. Keep the collection and season notation small, and use one oversized italic word or chapter number as a restrained graphic gesture.

### Inspiration and story

Place a short seasonal premise and three design principles beside a tactile moodboard and a vertical palette. Favor sensory and construction language over vague lifestyle adjectives.

### Color, fabric, and silhouette direction

Use three coordinated modules: proportional palette, fabric macro plus sourcing table, and a charred silhouette board. Explain how the elements form one design language.

### Hero looks and key pieces

Show three consistent full-length looks with number, garment composition, color or material, and role. Reserve a side card for the anchor piece and its verified product or commercial details.

### Consumer and wearing occasions

Pair a behavior-led consumer profile with four or fewer wardrobe occasions. Avoid treating a named fictional persona as validated research unless it is genuinely sourced.

### Launch and commercialization

Use a phased horizontal schedule, then commercial target cards and a channel-mix band. Connect editorial, wholesale, direct-to-consumer, retail, and made-to-order activity to available inventory and delivery dates.

## Imagery

- Use rights-cleared full-length studio portraits, garment details, fabric macros, atelier process, accessories, still life, fittings, and controlled location photography.
- Maintain consistent warm light, natural texture, realistic skin, and accurate garment color. Use a stable crop ratio within each image family.
- Image direction should reveal drape, proportion, construction, hand feel, and styling. Do not crop away the garment feature under discussion.
- Credit photographer, model, stylist, hair and makeup, location, and rights status where required.
- Avoid generic runway crowds, unrelated street style, stock shopping imagery, heavy beauty retouching, AI artifacts, and inconsistent seasonal color grading.

## Content integrity

- Do not invent materials, fiber composition, suppliers, certifications, garment count, prices, margins, assortment mix, persona data, orders, doors, placements, sell-through, revenue, channel mix, or launch dates.
- Distinguish design intention, approved sample, salesman sample, production-ready style, confirmed order, forecast, and target.
- Material and sustainability claims require traceable scope, certification, supplier, chain-of-custody, and applicable product coverage.
- Commercial metrics must state currency, wholesale or retail basis, gross or net revenue, returns, markdowns, inventory, delivery window, channel, and forecast scenario.
- Audience or occasion research must state market, sample, date, and method. Do not infer identity, income, or behavior from an image alone.
- Use approved product imagery and accurate color. Clearly label concept art, sample photography, or planned styles.
- If data is absent, omit it or label it `concept`, `sample`, `planned`, `target`, `forecast`, or `to be confirmed`. Never fabricate detail to make a lookbook feel complete.

## Avoid

- Do not copy preview collection names, narrative, moodboard, palette, fabrics, silhouettes, looks, models, prices, personas, markets, dates, or targets.
- Do not sacrifice garment visibility to oversized typography or decorative cropping.
- Do not turn the deck into either a pure art book with no launch logic or a spreadsheet with no design point of view.
- Do not overuse terracotta, italics, chapter numbers, or dark panels; their pacing creates the editorial rhythm.
- Do not use glossy gradients, glass cards, large rounded corners, drop shadows, 3D garment mockups, or generic luxury motifs.
- Do not present a forecast as an order, a sample as production, or a moodboard image as owned campaign imagery.
- Do not claim sustainability, craftsmanship, origin, or exclusivity without evidence and exact scope.
